title: Work handed out from a pool
question: In each as-needed pool, how was the spending shared among the members, which pools gave one member half or more, and which members received nothing?
finding: 64 pools with two or more members and enough spending to compare were found in Public Works’ monthly status reports, the Port’s contracting reports and the City’s contract file. In 17 of them one member took half or more of a pool of three or more, the most lopsided being Lee Incorporated with 81.3% of $7.1 million in "PUC Speclzed Tech AsNeeded Srv" (Public Utilities Commission; the pool name is the contract title as the City’s file abbreviates it). 26 member places across these pools show no spending at all. In Public Works’ own reports the widest gap is Smith-Emery San Francisco at 69.8% of "Special Inspection & Testing", against an even share of 20%. Neither department’s quoted rule promises rotation or an even split.
how: Public Works: the status report for the month ending 31 October 2026 gives each pool member’s master contract amount and amount expended to date. Members of one pool are grouped by contract generation (contracts ending within 300 days of each other); job-order contracts, which are separate contracts for one kind of work, are grouped by trade. Port: payments per contract in each fiscal year’s contracting report (fiscal 2016-17, first half of fiscal 2017-18, fiscal 2018-19, fiscal 2019-20, fiscal 2020-21, fiscal 2021-22), added up for the four pools whose tables parse cleanly. Other departments: contract titles in the City’s contract file that contain "as-needed", "pool", "on-call", "job order" or "master agreement" with three or more prime contractors and $1 million or more paid, as in the aliases analysis. An even share is one divided by the number of members; "times an even share" divides the largest member’s share by it. "JV" in a member’s name is the record’s short form for a joint venture. The owner-groups built by the aliases analysis were used to count sister companies as one entrant.
limits: What the rules say, as quoted in the download: Public Works, “Work will be authorized through individual Contract Service Orders based on project needs and available funding.”; Port, “Staff initiate a CSO to meet a specific need and the prime then forms a team, pulling from the subconsultants assembled at time of proposal.” Nothing quoted requires rotation, so an uneven split breaks no rule shown here. Uneven shares have ordinary causes: members were awarded contracts of different sizes (the capacity column shows the largest member’s share of the pool’s contract value), specialties differ inside one pool, a member may decline work, and one large project can absorb a contract. No department publishes a log of task orders (both call them Contract Service Orders), so the number and size of individual orders cannot be seen. Public Works figures are cumulative and a few fell from one month to the next, which suggests corrections. Port names are as printed, so one firm under two different names appears twice. Newly awarded generations with under $500,000 spent are left out as too young to judge. In the City’s contract file a zero means no payment is recorded, and members whose contracts began later have had less time to be paid.
